items.title: Pulsed radiofrequency magnetic fields may disorient migratory birds, experiments suggest
items.summary: Every year, millions of migratory birds travel between different geographical regions on Earth to find food, escape cold weather or reach safe environments to raise chicks. items.title: Dodo birds more clever than we thought
items.summary: The Mauritian dodo—a global symbol of human-caused extinction and one of the world's largest pigeons—may not have deserved its reputation as a silly simpleton and may have been the only member of its group to live in the dark.

items.title: Meteorite that smashed through a New Jersey roof reveals clues to life’s origins
items.summary: A rare meteorite that crashed through a New Jersey roof contains evidence of ancient salty fluids, organic compounds, and amino acids from a primitive asteroid. Its pristine chemistry could offer new clues about how space rocks helped supply early Earth with some of the ingredients needed for life.

items.title: How winter canola could profit Illinois farmers, improve sustainability
items.summary: A new simulation study from the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign suggests winter canola could be profitable and environmentally beneficial if added to a conventional corn-soy rotation in the U.S. Midwest.

items.title: New fuel cell breakthrough could help power energy-hungry data centers
items.summary: A new nanostructured carbon design lets fuel-cell catalysts use tiny amounts of platinum while remaining remarkably stable and efficient. The breakthrough could help hydrogen fuel cells become a more practical way to power data centers, vehicles, and other energy-intensive technologies.

items.title: Dodos probably weren't as stupid as historians made them out to be: new research
items.summary: The dodo has been extinct for more than 300 years, wiped out within decades of humans arriving on its home island of Mauritius, but it lives on in the public imagination.

items.title: Scientists reveal how much exercise you really need to protect your heart
items.summary: Getting the recommended 150 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous exercise each week may offer only modest protection against heart attacks and strokes. items.summary: A protein that evolved long before the human circulatory system may help unlock stronger cancer treatments. items.title: Reduced gravity pushes people toward simpler movement patterns, experiments suggest
items.summary: From reaching for a cup of coffee to tying your shoelaces, gravity shapes nearly all human movement. So how do our bodies react when that familiar force begins to change? Texas A&M University researchers are exploring the answer through a multiphase project supported by NASA.

items.summary: Scientists have discovered incredibly tiny plasma whirlpools swirling across the Sun’s surface, some just 20 kilometers wide. items.title: Cutting sweet foods doesn’t curb cravings or improve health
items.summary: Changing how much sweet-tasting food people eat may not change how much they crave or enjoy sweetness after all. items.title: Swarms of tiny robots remove microplastics from soil and water
items.summary: Microplastics, which are plastic particles under 5 millimeters, are a major and growing threat in both soil and water. They damage soil fertility, disrupt nutrient cycling, harm aquatic and terrestrial life, and can move through the food chain. That makes cleaning them up an urgent priority.

items.title: Canada tries to adapt to a future of wildfires
items.summary: Faced with another summer when wildfires have scorched millions of hectares of land and blankets of smoke have disrupted daily life nationwide, Canada is trying to limit the annual devastation.

items.title: Loneliness may damage health in ways isolation does not: New study
items.summary: You can spend every day surrounded by other people and still feel lonely. You can also spend long periods alone without finding the experience distressing.

items.title: Nocturnal 'coffee frog' discovered in Costa Rica
items.summary: A tiny greenish, nocturnal frog that thrives in coffee plantations has been discovered in Costa Rica's central Pacific region, where it also faces risks from agrochemicals used in farming.

items.title: Teen cannabis use linked to slower memory and thinking growth
items.summary: Teens who start using cannabis may experience slower growth in memory, attention, language, and processing speed. Their abilities often developed normally at first, then began leveling off while nonusers continued improving. THC appeared to be the most likely driver, especially for worsening memory.

items.summary: By rapidly twisting a microscopically small tip back and forth, researchers at the University of Maryland (UMD) have unlocked a new way to detect subtle changes on the surface of a material flexing in response to infrared light.

items.title: Hidden anatomy of clouds reveals how rain may begin without ice crystals
items.summary: The initiation of rain in clouds without ice remains one of the largest unsolved mysteries in atmospheric science.

items.title: Laser spectroscopy helps reveal hidden nuclear properties in fermium
items.summary: For the first time, researchers have determined the shape of the actinide nucleus of fermium-255 and measured its structure with high precision and resolution.

items.summary: When most baby turtles hatch, their sex depends on the temperature of the sand or soil where their mother laid her eggs. Warm incubation produces females, while cool nests produce males.

items.summary: A new genomic resource from the Texas A&M AgriLife Research plant genomics team is providing a powerful new foundation for faster, more precise turfgrass genetics and breeding. The team discovered a breakthrough genome that finally reveals the full genetic blueprint of zoysia grass.

items.summary: In the animal kingdom, only those that adapt to their environment survive. This adaptation takes a wide range of forms, from invisible internal shifts in gene expression to dramatic anatomical changes, such as tadpoles growing legs and transitioning to life on land as frogs.

items.title: Birdsong and whale song show patterns similar to human language
items.summary: An international team of researchers has uncovered a previously undetected structure in the birdsong of Bengalese finches that has the same statistical patterns found in human languages.
